lead: Physical design names the actual things and devices in an IoT system and the parts inside them. It answers the hardware question: what is this made of? A thing is a physical object with an identity. A device is the engineered package that adds sensing, computation, communication and action. Every deployment uses this layer: a soil-moisture node, a smart meter, an RFID-tagged parcel. The choices made here fix cost, size and battery life before any software is written.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for what IoT is and why identifiable things matter.

blocks.text: Physical design is the hardware answer to a simple question: what is this IoT thing made of? It lists the parts, their package, their power supply and their connections. It does not describe what functions the system performs; that is the logical design.

A thing is a physical object with an identity. The identity may be an RFID tag on a parcel, a serial number in a chip, or a network address. A device is the engineering package that gives a thing sensing, computation, communication and action. One thing may contain several devices. A smart water meter is a thing; inside it, the electronics box with a flow sensor, a microcontroller, a radio module and a battery is the device.
A gateway is a device that collects data from many things and forwards it to the internet. It is the bridge between short-range radios and the wide-area network.

The physical design fixes the bill of materials: which sensor, which control unit, which radio, which battery. It also fixes the enclosure and the duty cycle. Those choices decide cost, size and battery life.

sections.h3: Five parts of an IoT device

blocks.text: Every active IoT device has five jobs, and usually five parts.

The control unit runs the logic. It reads sensors, decides, drives actuators and formats data for the radio. A microcontroller is a small chip with memory and input/output pins; an Arduino board and an ESP8266 module are common microcontroller examples. A single-board computer such as Raspberry Pi runs an operating system and is used when more computing is needed. Programming these boards is covered in Unit 4.

Sensors convert a physical quantity into an electrical signal. A soil-moisture sensor gives a voltage that depends on water content. Actuators convert an electrical signal into action: a relay switches a pump, a motor opens a valve.
The communication module sends data to a gateway or a cloud. It may use Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy, LoRa or a cellular link. Radio standards are in Unit 3.
The power source supplies energy. Mains power is used where wiring exists. Batteries are used where it does not. Energy harvesting takes small amounts of power from light, vibration or heat.

A passive RFID tag is a special case: it has an antenna and a chip but no battery. The reader's radio wave powers it. It is a thing with identity, but it is not a full device with sensing and actuation.

The first calculation in physical design is the power budget. A device rarely runs at full current all the time. It wakes, measures, transmits and sleeps. The duty cycle is the fraction of time spent active.

blocks.where: I<sub>avg</sub> is the average current in mA; I<sub>active</sub> is the active current in mA; t<sub>active</sub> is the active time in seconds; I<sub>sleep</sub> is the sleep current in mA; t<sub>sleep</sub> is the sleep time in seconds; T = t<sub>active</sub> + t<sub>sleep</sub> is the period in seconds.
Life is the battery life in hours; Capacity is the battery capacity in mAh; I<sub>avg</sub> is the average current in mA.

blocks.text: Use the same unit for every current. 20 µA = 0.02 mA. Ignore conversion loss unless the question gives an efficiency.

figure.caption: The worked example laid out step by step. The orange step is the unit trap the chapter warns about: 20 µA must become 0.02 mA before averaging; the last box is the result — 0.0367 mA average current, about 54,500 hours or 6.2 years.

spec.title: Power budget of the soil-moisture node
spec.aria: A six-step flow computing the power budget of a soil-moisture node: period 3600 s with 2 s active and 3598 s asleep, sleep current converted to 0.02 mA, 131.96 mA·s of charge per period, 0.0367 mA average current, 54,500 hours of battery life, and 6.2 years.

examples.question: A soil-moisture node uses a 3.7 V, 2,000 mAh battery. Sleep current is 20 µA. Active current is 30 mA for 2 s every 1 hour. Estimate the average current and the battery life. Ignore conversion loss.
steps: Write the period T = 1 hour = 3600 s. Active time t<sub>active</sub> = 2 s. Sleep time t<sub>sleep</sub> = 3600 − 2 = 3598 s.
Convert sleep current to mA: 20 µA = 0.02 mA.
Active charge per period = 30 mA × 2 s = 60 mA·s. Sleep charge per period = 0.02 mA × 3598 s = 71.96 mA·s.
Total charge per period = 60 + 71.96 = 131.96 mA·s. Average current = 131.96 mA·s ÷ 3600 s = 0.03666 mA ≈ 0.0367 mA.
In years: 54495.9 h ÷ 8760 h/year = 6.22 years ≈ 6.2 years.
examples.answer: Average current ≈ 0.0367 mA; battery life ≈ 54,500 h ≈ 6.2 years.
examples.check:
capacity = 2000
I_active = 30
t_active = 2
I_sleep = 0.02
T = 3600
t_sleep = T - t_active
I_avg = (I_active * t_active + I_sleep * t_sleep) / T
I_avg_rounded = round(I_avg, 4)
life = capacity / I_avg_rounded
years = life / 8760
print(I_avg_rounded)
print(round(life, 1))
print(round(years, 2))

traps: Do not confuse physical design with logical design. Physical design is the hardware parts; logical design is the functions the system performs.
A sensor alone is not an IoT system. It needs a control unit, a communication module and a power source to become a device.
Mix mA and µA at your peril. 20 µA is 0.02 mA, not 20 mA. Convert every current to the same unit before averaging.
Average current is not active current. A device that wakes for 2 s in an hour spends almost all its time asleep, so the sleep current can dominate the average.
A passive RFID tag has no battery. The reader supplies its power. Do not call it a full device with sensing and actuation.

quiz.q: Define thing and device in IoT.
quiz.a: A thing is a physical object with an identity. A device is the engineering package that gives a thing sensing, computation, communication and action.

quiz.q: Why is a gateway needed in many IoT deployments?
quiz.a: Many things use short-range radios. A gateway collects their data and forwards it to the internet over a wide-area link, so the things do not each need a cellular module.

quiz.q: A device draws 50 mA for 1 s every 10 minutes. Sleep current is 10 µA. The battery is 1,000 mAh. Estimate the battery life in hours and years.
quiz.a: T = 600 s. t<sub>active</sub> = 1 s, t<sub>sleep</sub> = 599 s. Sleep current = 0.01 mA. Average current = (50×1 + 0.01×599) ÷ 600 = 55.99 ÷ 600 = 0.09332 mA. Life = 1000 ÷ 0.09332 = 10715 h ≈ 1.22 years.

quiz.q: A passive RFID tag has no battery. Is it an IoT device? Explain.
quiz.a: It is a thing with identity, but it is not a full device. It has no control unit, no sensor and no power source of its own; the reader powers it. It becomes part of an IoT system when a reader and a network use its identity.

quiz.q: Convert a 3.7 V, 2,000 mAh battery to watt-hours.
List the five parts of an active IoT device and one job of each.
quiz.a: Control unit runs logic; sensors measure state; actuators change state; communication module sends data; power source supplies energy.

quiz.q: Design A sends data every 1 minute; Design B sends every 10 minutes. Both use the same radio and battery. Which lasts longer and why?
quiz.a: Design B lasts longer. Longer sleep time lowers the average current because the active current is a smaller fraction of the period. Battery life is capacity divided by average current.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving toward battery-free and energy-harvesting nodes, system-on-chip designs that combine a microcontroller and a radio, and edge processing that reduces radio time. Research explores wake-up radios and backscatter communication. Search for low-power IoT node design, energy harvesting wireless sensor, passive RFID tag, and microcontroller sleep modes.
